name: Yemeni states (Zaydi imamate and others)
summary: The states of Yemen and Hadramaut, including the Zaydi imamate (897–1962) and dynasties such as the Rasulids, famous for coffee and tall mud-brick towns.

knownFor.label: Mocha coffee
knownFor.note: Coffee traded through the port of Mocha.

knownFor.label: Shibam
knownFor.note: The “Manhattan of the desert”, mud-brick towers.

location.value: The south-western corner of Arabia: the Yemen highlands, the Red Sea coast (Tihama) and Hadramaut.

terrain.value: High mountains with terraced fields, coastal plains and the deep Hadramaut valley.

climate.value: Monsoon summer rains in the highlands make it the greenest part of Arabia; the coast is hot and dry.

resources.value: Coffee (from the 1400s), frankincense, grain grown on terraces, and trade through Red Sea ports.

urbanisation.value: Sanaa, Zabid, Taiz, Mocha and the tower-house town of Shibam.

disease.value: Plague, malaria on the coast and famine-related disease.

migration.value: Hadramis traded and settled across the Indian Ocean.

economicBase.value: Terrace farming and trade, especially coffee from about 1450 to 1720.

tradeRoutes.value: Coffee shipped from Mocha to Egypt, the Ottoman Empire, India and Europe.

wealth.value: The coffee trade made Mocha rich in the 1600s.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver and copper coins; taxes on harvests and trade.

inequality.value: Sayyid families and tribal sheikhs above farmers and servants.

governmentType.value: The Zaydi imamate in the highlands, alongside Sunni dynasties (Rasulids, Tahirids) and sultanates in the south.

keyRulers.value: Al-Hadi ila’l-Haqq (founder, 897); al-Mansur Umar (Rasulid, 1229); Imam Yahya (1904–48).

succession.value: Imams chosen from the Prophet’s descendants.

institutions.value: Zaydi religious law; the imam was chosen from the Prophet’s family for learning and leadership.

stability.value: Often divided between rival imams, dynasties and tribes.

eliteConflict.value: Rival claimants to the imamate and tribal confederations.

armyAndTech.value: Tribal levies; later rifles and Ottoman-style troops.

territoryChange.value: Ottomans ruled parts of Yemen twice (1538–1635, 1849–1918); Britain took Aden in 1839.

alliancesRivals.value: Ottoman Empire, Britain in Aden, and the Saudis to the north.

inventions.value: Early coffee drinking (Sufi houses, 1400s) spread from Yemen.

scienceEducation.value: Zabid was a famous centre of Islamic learning; Rasulid sultans wrote on astronomy and farming.

openness.value: Open through ports; the imamate under Yahya (1918–48) was very closed.

communicationTransport.value: Camels, mountain paths and Red Sea ships.

religion.value: Zaydi Shia Islam in the north, Sunni (Shafi’i) Islam in the south and coast.

artsArchitecture.value: Tower houses of Sanaa and Shibam, built of stone and mud brick.

socialStructure.value: Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet), tribes, townspeople and farmers.

dailyLife.value: Multi-storey mud-brick houses; bread, honey, coffee.

neighbours.value: Hejaz, Oman, Ottoman Empire, Ethiopia across the Red Sea.

ideasReligions.value: Islam to Southeast Asia via Hadrami traders.

declineSignals.value: Loss of the coffee monopoly to Java and the Caribbean (1700s).

outcome.value: The imamate was overthrown in the 1962 revolution.
